interest: For historians, this file provides an extraordinarily granular, month-by-month record of the pivotal year 1939, capturing Japanese domestic politics and wartime state-building alongside real-time American diplomatic observations. It is particularly valuable for its dual perspective: the exhaustive on-the-ground political and economic reporting drafted by Tokyo embassy staff (such as Third Secretary James Espy) juxtaposed directly with Washington's internal Division of Far Eastern Affairs memoranda assessing report utility, distribution, and brevity. Furthermore, the extensive chronological registers of embassy despatches and telegrams appended to the reports serve as a comprehensive index of bilateral diplomacy, tracking specific American protests over treaty rights, missionary property damage in China, the termination of the 1911 commercial treaty, and the diplomatic shockwaves rippling from the Molotov-Ribbentrop Pact and the outbreak of war in Europe.
overview: This file constitutes part 2 of the U.S. State Department’s internal affairs records on Japan for 1938–1939 (Decimal File 894.00, File 1169), primarily comprising the American Embassy in Tokyo’s exhaustive monthly political and economic reports (Reports Nos. 148 through 157) covering January through November 1939. Transmitted under Ambassador Joseph C. Grew and accompanied by evaluative memoranda from the State Department’s Division of Far Eastern Affairs, these records document Japan's internal political shifts—from the installation and fall of the Hiranuma Cabinet to the emergence of the Abe Cabinet—alongside sweeping wartime regimentation under the National General Mobilization Law, soaring inflation, and resource shortages. Externally, the documents track escalating Japanese military operations in China, the annexation of the Spratly Islands and occupation of Hainan, aerial bombings of third-power mission properties, blockades and friction in foreign concessions (notably Kulangsu, Shanghai, and Tientsin), severe border fighting with Soviet-Mongolian forces at Nomonhan, the diplomatic shock of the German-Soviet Non-Aggression Pact, and deteriorating Japanese-American relations punctuated by the U.S. abrogation of the 1911 Treaty of Commerce and Navigation and Ambassador Grew’s blunt October 1939 address.
